pages.name: A start and a direction
pages.text: A line in space is a start point plus any amount of one direction. Write the start as p and the direction as v. A point on the line is `r = p + t v`, where t is any number. At `t = 0` you are at the start. Each extra unit of t adds one more v. Take `p = (0, 1, 0)` and `v = (1, 2, 0)`. At `t = 2` the dot is at `(0, 1, 0)` + `(2, 4, 0)` = `(2, 5, 0)`.

pages.name: Where at t = 3?
pages.task: The line is `(0, 1, 0) + t(1, 2, 0)`. Where is the dot at `t = 3`?
pages.why: A point on the line is `p + t v`. At `t = 3` that is `(0, 1, 0)` + `(3, 6, 0)` = `(3, 7, 0)`.

pages.name: Through two points
pages.text: For the line through two points A and B, the direction is the step between them, B − A. Here `A = (1, 0, 2)` and `B = (3, 4, 0)`, so `B − A = (2, 4, −2)`. B − A is the whole step from A to B. So for t from 0 to 1, `A + t(B − A)` is a fraction t of the way along. `t = ½` gives the midpoint, `(2, 2, 1)`.
pages.alt: A 3-D view with x, y and z axes. B minus A is (2, 4, minus 2). Dot r is (2, 2, 1).

pages.name: Which direction?
pages.task: A line runs through `A = (2, 1, 1)` and `B = (5, 3, 1)`. Which arrow is a direction for it?
pages.why: The direction is the step between the points. `B − A` = `(5 − 2, 3 − 1, 1 − 1)` = `(3, 2, 0)`.

pages.name: A plane and its normal
pages.text: A plane has a start point p and one arrow n square to it, its [[normal]]. Square means at right angles to every line in the plane. The plane is every point whose step from p is square to n. Take `p = (1, 1, 3)` and `n = (2, 1, 2)`. The test point `r = (2, 1, 2)` is a step of `(1, 0, −1)` from p. So `n · (r − p) = 2 + 0 − 2 = 0`. Off the plane, the reading is plus on n’s side and minus on the other.

pages.task: The plane runs through `p = (1, 1, 3)` with normal `n = (2, 1, 2)`. Which point lies on it?
pages.why: A point is on the plane when its step from p is square to n. For `(1, 3, 2)` the step is `(0, 2, −1)`. Then `n · (0, 2, −1)` = `0 + 2 − 2` = `0`. In `2x + y + 2z = 9` it gives `2 + 3 + 4 = 9`.

pages.name: Its equation
pages.text: A plane’s equation has the normal’s parts in front of x, y and z. Write `r = (x, y, z)`, so r − p = (x − 1, y − 1, z − 3). Dot that with n and set it to 0. That gives `2x + y + 2z = 9`, where 9 is `n · p`. Sliding within the plane leaves the reading unchanged. So the straight route to the plane runs along n, and the reading is |n| times its length. `|n| = 3` and the origin reads −9. So the origin is `9 ÷ 3 = 3` from the plane.

pages.name: Which equation?
pages.task: A plane passes through `(1, 2, 0)` with normal `(3, −1, 2)`. Which is its equation?
pages.why: The normal’s parts go in front of x, y and z. So the plane is `3x − y + 2z = d`. The point `(1, 2, 0)` gives `d = 3 − 2 + 0 = 1`.

pages.name: Two directions
pages.text: The same plane can come from two directions that lie in it. Take `u = (1, 0, −1)` and `w = (0, 2, −1)`. All the mixes s u + t w fill a plane through the origin. Add p, and that plane slides to the start, `r = p + s u + t w`. The paint marks each point the dot reaches. The cross product `u × w` is square to both u and w, so it is a normal. Here it is `(2, 1, 2)`, the same normal as before.

pages.name: Which normal?
pages.task: A plane holds the directions `(1, 1, 0)` and `(0, 1, 1)`. Which arrow is a normal to it?
pages.why: A normal must be square to both directions. The cross product gives one. `(1, 1, 0) × (0, 1, 1)` = `(1, −1, 1)`. Check it. Its dot product with each direction is 0.

pages.name: Where they meet
pages.text: To find where a line meets a plane, put the line’s point into the equation and solve for t. On `(0, 1, 0) + t(1, 2, 0)` the point is `(t, 1 + 2t, 0)`. In `2x + y + 2z = 9` that gives `2t + (1 + 2t) + 0 = 9`. So `t = 2`, and they meet at `(2, 5, 0)`. Each unit of t changes the reading `n · (r − p)` by `n · v`, here 4. If `n · v` is 0, the line runs parallel to the plane.

pages.task: The planes `x + y + z = 5` and `x − y = 0` meet in a line. Which way does it run?
pages.why: The line lies in both planes. So its direction is square to both normals. The cross product gives such an arrow. `(1, 1, 1) × (1, −1, 0)` = `(1, 1, −2)`. Check it. `1 + 1 − 2 = 0` and `1 − 1 + 0 = 0`.
